column1:
Hawkish policy stance remains the dominant signal (75 bp hike, “ongoing increases” toward a “sufficiently restrictive” stance, continued QT, higher IOER), but the latest SLOOS points to a meaningful tightening in bank credit that tempers the hawkish read.

SLOOS cross-check:
- Supply tightens broadly: Banks reported tightening standards for C&I loans (including foreign banks) and across CRE segments (construction/land development, nonfarm nonresidential, multifamily), and tighter standards across residential mortgages (QM/non-QM jumbo, subprime) and consumer credit (credit cards; consumer loans overall).
- Demand is weakening: Banks reported weaker demand for C&I loans from large, middle-market, and small firms; weaker demand for auto and credit card loans; consumer-loan demand largely unchanged overall; stronger demand for HELOCs is a partial offset.
- Underwriting and risk appetite: Banks less likely to approve lower-FICO applications (e.g., 620/680) and more likely to approve high FICO (720), citing the economic outlook as a key reason for tightening.
- Macro risk assessment: Banks elevated the likelihood of recession, and customer financing needs (AR/inventory) were cited as drivers of demand shifts.

Implication: With the bank-lending channel already tightening and demand softening, financial conditions are doing additional work for the Fed. That supports the statement’s emphasis on “cumulative tightening” and policy lags, and warrants a modestly less hawkish interpretation than a pure rate/QT read.

Adjusted sentiment: Still hawkish, but moderated by SLOOS-confirmed credit tightening and softer loan demand.
